content: Among very low birth weight (VLBW) infants, early neonatal hyperglycemia is a frequent occurrence and is associated with an increased risk of mortality and significant morbidities. However, it remains unclear whether hyperglycemia itself directly causes these adverse clinical outcomes or whether preventing hyperglycemia can improve these outcomes. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of interventions aimed at preventing hyperglycemia in VLBW neonates who are receiving either full or partial parenteral nutrition. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to April 2011. Additionally, abstracts from relevant pediatric research conferences were reviewed. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated interventions to prevent hyperglycemia in neonates with a birth weight of less than 1500 grams or a gestational age of less than 32 weeks. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data on study design, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes, and evaluated the methodological quality of the included trials. The treatment effects were measured using relative risk and risk difference for categorical outcomes, and mean difference for continuous outcomes, all reported with 95% confidence intervals. Four trials met the inclusion criteria. Two of these trials compared lower versus higher rates of glucose infusion during the early postnatal period. However, these trials were too small to provide reliable evidence regarding their effects on mortality or major morbidities. The other two trials, one of which was a moderately large multicenter trial (NIRTURE, Beardsall 2008), compared insulin infusion with standard care. Insulin infusion was found to reduce hyperglycemia but was associated with an increased risk of death before 28 days and a higher incidence of hypoglycemia. Importantly, while insulin infusion reduced hyperglycemia, it did not result in significant improvements in major morbidities. The long-term effects on neurodevelopment remain to be determined. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to guide clinical practice regarding the optimal glucose infusion rate in VLBW neonates. Large, well-powered randomized trials are needed to assess the effects of different glucose infusion rates on clinical outcomes, including mortality, major morbidities, and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. Regarding insulin infusion, the evidence does not support its routine use to prevent hyperglycemia in VLBW neonates. Further randomized trials of insulin infusion may be warranted, particularly in extremely low birth weight neonates who are at a very high risk of hyperglycemia and neonatal death. Such trials should consider the use of validated real-time glucose monitoring systems and refined algorithms to achieve tight glucose control within the target range.
